faqs.question: What do you write in a love letter for your girlfriend in Assamese?
faqs.answer: Settle two things before the words: the second-person pronoun (তুমি is the safe default over তই and আপুনি) and whether you are spelling with the Assamese ৰ rather than the Bangla র. After that, short and specific beats long and ornamental — name a real day, a real habit of hers, and one thing you have not said out loud.

faqs.question: Should I use তুমি or তই in a love letter to my girlfriend?
faqs.answer: তুমি. English Wiktionary labels তুমি "familiar" and তই "very familiar, inferior", and that downward tilt on তই lands as intimacy in some families and as rudeness in others. Many couples do use তই, so if she uses it with you, use it back — but remember that switching re-conjugates every verb.

faqs.question: What is the difference between ৰ and র?
faqs.answer: They are different Unicode characters for the same sound in two different languages. ৰ is U+09F0, which the Unicode Standard names as the Assamese letter ra; র is U+09B0, the Bangla letter ra. Assamese writes মৰম and তোমাৰ; text that has defaulted to Bangla writes মরম and তোমার, which reads as the wrong language.

faqs.question: How do you say "I love you" in Assamese?
faqs.answer: মই তোমাক ভালপাওঁ — moi tomak bhalpau. This appears verbatim as the usage example on English Wiktionary's ভালপোৱা entry, which gives the scholarly transliteration moi tümak bhalpaü̃ and the pronunciation /bʱal.pʊa/. তোমাক is the objective form of তুমি, so the line is already in the neutral-affectionate register.

faqs.question: What does মৰম mean?
faqs.answer: মৰম (morom) is glossed by Wiktionary as love, strong affection, caress, a kiss from a child, fondness and friendship, from Sanskrit मर्मन्. It is softer and more usable than a declaration, which makes it the most valuable single noun in an Assamese love letter. Note the ৰ — it is the word most often mis-spelled as মরম.

faqs.question: Can I use Google Translate for an Assamese love letter?
faqs.answer: It is a bad idea, for a specific reason. Assamese is genuinely low-resource: in Scientific Reports in March 2026, Nath and Gulzar report that the scarcity of parallel corpora is the core constraint, and their zero-shot system reaches BLEU 28.65 by routing English through Bengali. A consumer translator has none of that engineering behind it.

faqs.question: Should I write in Assamese script or in Roman letters?
faqs.answer: Stack the script above a romanisation if she reads Assamese but types in Latin, which is very common. Script alone is best only when you know her phone renders Assamese — 50.3% of our 41,486 recorded views open on a phone, and a missing font fails silently rather than visibly.

faqs.question: How long should a short love letter for girlfriend in Assamese be?
faqs.answer: Three to five sentences is plenty, and one verified line beats five unverified ones. The constraint is not length but accuracy: every sentence you cannot check is a sentence that might read as machine output. A short letter with correct ৰ and ৱ lands better than a long one full of Bangla defaults.

faqs.question: Is Assamese the same as Bengali?
faqs.answer: No. Both are Eastern Indo-Aryan and share a writing system that Unicode encodes in one block, but Assamese adds ৰ (U+09F0) and ৱ (U+09F1), and it has sounds Bengali lacks — Mahanta's IPA illustration documents /x/ as a full phoneme and exactly one rhotic. Treating them as interchangeable is the error this whole topic turns on.

faqs.question: What is the Assamese word for a letter?
faqs.answer: চিঠি (sithi) is the everyday word for a written letter. খত and পত্ৰ also exist, and Wiktionary marks both as uncommon. Wiktionary's example sentence uses the classifier -খন: এই চিঠিখন কেতিয়া পাবগৈ? — "When will this letter arrive?"

faqs.question: How do I check my Assamese if I am not a native speaker?
faqs.answer: Verify each line against a dictionary entry rather than a translator, then have one native speaker read the finished letter. As a mechanical check you can run yourself, search your text for র — Assamese never uses it, so every hit is a mistake. That one search catches the most common error.

faqs.question: What makes a romantic love letter for girlfriend in Assamese feel personal rather than copied?
faqs.answer: Specifics she can verify. Sample letters are generic by construction, which is why they read as templates — every page ranking for this query hands you the same interchangeable paragraphs. Build from verified words instead and put one concrete memory in, and the register does the rest.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Love Letter for Girlfriend in Assamese: ৰ, ৱ and "You"

A love letter for girlfriend in Assamese turns on two decisions you make before writing a line: which second-person "you" you use — তই (*toi*), তুমি (*tumi*) or আপুনি (*apuni*) — and whether you spell it with the two letters that exist only in Assamese, ৰ and ৱ, instead of the Bangla র a phone keyboard or translator will quietly hand you. For scale on the format, the "I love you" page is the most-created thing on SubhSandesh: 987 pages, 29.2% of all 3,377 built since 2026-03-12, with a median 7.2 hours between a creator's first save and last edit across those 987 pages.

Nobody writes one in one sitting. Below: the pronoun, the two letters, five verified building blocks, and when Assamese is the wrong call.

## What makes a letter Assamese rather than generically Indic

An Assamese love letter is a letter written in Assamese — অসমীয়া (*oxomia*) — an Eastern Indo-Aryan language and the official language of Assam. The word for the letter itself is চিঠি (*sithi*); খত and পত্ৰ exist too, both marked uncommon.

What marks it as Assamese is narrower than most people expect. It shares its writing system with Bangla, and Unicode puts both in one block — but Assamese adds characters and carries sounds Bangla does not. The [IPA illustration of Assamese by Shakuntala Mahanta](https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/FD4090937A7BC4318FCF1117E82313E4/S0025100312000096a.pdf/div-class-title-assamese-div.pdf), in the *Journal of the International Phonetic Association* in 2012, documents the velar fricative /x/ as a full phoneme, exactly one rhotic, and no distinctive affricates — which is why the language name romanises as *oxomia*, not *asomia*.

## Which "you" you use: তই, তুমি or আপুনি

Assamese has three second-person singular pronouns and they are not interchangeable. তই (*toi*) is very familiar, তুমি (*tumi*) is familiar, আপুনি (*apuni*) is formal.

**Use তুমি.** আপুনি is for a stranger or an elder; sent to a girlfriend it reads as distance or as a joke. তই is genuinely used between couples in many families, but its dictionary label is "very familiar, inferior" — a downward tilt that lands as intimacy or rudeness depending on the household you are writing into. তুমি is warm without gambling. That is a judgement from dictionary labels, not from living inside the language, so treat it as a default to check.

Now the part almost nobody mentions: swapping the pronoun is not a find-and-replace, because Assamese puts the person on the verb. In ["Pro-drop and subject pronouns in Assamese"](https://www.al-kindipublisher.com/index.php/ijllt/article/download/1040/841), published open-access under CC BY in the *International Journal of Linguistics, Literature and Translation* in 2020, Radhika Boruah of the Centre for Endangered Languages at Tezpur University tabulates the verb *kha* ("eat") across all nine personal pronouns.

With তুমি the past and future are *kha-l-a* and *kha-b-a*; with তই, *kha-l-i* and *kha-b-i*. Change the pronoun and every verb ending changes with it.

Boruah carries a second finding worth acting on: Assamese is pro-drop, so most subject pronouns can be dropped, but she reports this is "not acceptable in written language." A letter is written language. Keep the pronoun in.

## ৰ and ৱ: the two letters that separate Assamese from Bangla

This is the most common error non-speakers make, and it is fully specified, not a matter of taste. Chapter 12 of [the Unicode Standard, version 16.0](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode16.0.0/core-spec/chapter-12/), released 10 September 2024, states that "Assamese employs two letters not used for the Bangla language": *ra* is U+09F0 ৰ, RA WITH MIDDLE DIAGONAL, and *wa* is U+09F1 ৱ, RA WITH LOWER DIAGONAL.

The two behave differently, and this is where guides get it wrong. ৰ is a straight replacement: Assamese does not use র at all, so every র in your text is an error. ৱ is an addition, for the /w/ sound — Assamese keeps ব (U+09AC) for /b/, in words like পাব and বেয়া.

So Assamese writes মৰম and তোমাৰ where Bangla-defaulted text writes মরম and তোমার. To a reader in Assam that is wrong in a way an apology cannot fix: it looks like you did not know which language you were writing.

Two consequences: your phone's Bangla keyboard may not expose ৰ and ৱ, so install an Asamiya layout; and search for র before sending, because every hit is a mistake.

This is not stylistic fussiness in Assam. In ["Language, Identity and Conflict"](https://www.spaceandculture.in/index.php/spaceandculture/article/view/1625), published CC BY in *Space and Culture, India* on 29 November 2024, Debajyoti Biswas of Bodoland University draws on interviews with 150 families in western Assam and traces the Language Movement of 1960, the Medium of Instruction Movement of 1972 and the Assam Movement of 1979–85, finding that conflict over language intensified tensions between Bengali- and Assamese-speaking communities. One character separates writing to her in her language from writing in a near-neighbour's.

## Five verified building blocks, with script and romanisation

Each comes from an English Wiktionary Assamese entry, which is why I can hand it over. I am deliberately not giving you a finished letter to copy: every page ranking for this query already does, and a paragraph someone else composed is a greeting card with your name on it.

The romanisation is a reading aid, not ISO 15919. চ and ছ are written *s*, স/শ/ষ as *x*, জ/য as *z*, ৰ as *r*, ৱ as *w* — following Mahanta's finding that Assamese has no distinctive affricates and contrasts /s/, /z/ and /x/.

### 1. মই তোমাক ভালপাওঁ — *moi tomak bhalpau*

"I love you." The whole job in four words, and it appears verbatim as the usage example on Wiktionary's [ভালপোৱা entry](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/ভালপোৱা), with the scholarly transliteration *moi tümak bhalpaü̃* and the pronunciation /bʱal.pʊa/. The ওঁ is nasalised. তোমাক is the objective form of তুমি, so the line is already in the register chosen above.

### 2. তুমি ভালে আছা নে — *tumi bhale asa ne*

"Are you well?" Wiktionary's তুমি entry carries this as its usage example, glossed "Are you good?". It is the opening a letter wants, because it asks rather than announces, and the আছা ending belongs to তুমি — Boruah's table shows তই taking *-i* endings where তুমি takes *-a*.

### 3. মৰম — *morom*

The word for the feeling when "love" is too large for the sentence. Wiktionary glosses মৰম as love, strong affection, caress, a kiss from a child, fondness and friendship, from Sanskrit मर्मन्. Note the ৰ: the word most often mis-spelled as মরম.

### 4. আদৰ — *ador*

Love and affection, and also respect and honour — a borrowing from Sanskrit आदर. Where মৰম is tender, আদৰ carries regard: for saying you value her, not that you want her.

### 5. জীৱন — *ziwon*

"Life." Spelled with ৱ, where Bangla writes the same word with ব. Wiktionary records two pronunciations: an inherited one without the intervocalic consonant, and a borrowed Sanskritic one with it.

## Script, romanisation, or both

Format is a real decision, and where our numbers are worth something.

| Format | What she receives | Main risk | Our data |
|---|---|---|---|
| Script only | মই তোমাক ভালপাওঁ | Fails silently if the Assamese font is missing | 50.3% of our 41,486 views open on a phone |
| Romanised only | moi tomak bhalpau | ৰ (U+09F0) and ৱ (U+09F1) vanish | 14,607 love-gf views, none tagged by script — we do not record it |
| Script above romanisation | both lines, stacked | Roughly doubles every line | 7.2 hours median first save to last edit, n=987 |
| Both, on a shareable page | the letter typed out on screen | Needs a link and a connection | 987 pages built, 29.2% of 3,377 |

Stack script above romanisation if she reads Assamese but types in Latin, which is common; send script alone only if you know her phone renders it.

Once the words are settled the container is a smaller decision. The [romantic "I love you" page](https://subhsandesh.in/love-gf) types the letter out on its cover, with a Love Quiz, a Truth or Dare round and an "Our Story" timeline behind it.

If your letter is darker than that, the [Darling romantic page](https://subhsandesh.in/darling) suits that register — fourth most-created here at 349 pages, 10.3% of the total. [Browse the full template set](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) if neither fits.

## Why machine translation gets Assamese wrong

Do not run the letter through a translator. Assamese is genuinely low-resource, and the systems that work best on it get there by going through Bangla.

In ["Zero-shot English–Assamese neural machine translation"](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-44209-w), published open-access in *Scientific Reports* on 17 March 2026, Basab Nath and Yonis Gulzar report that NMT for low-resource languages such as Assamese is held back by the scarcity of parallel corpora, and build a system exploiting Assamese–Bangla proximity to translate English to Assamese with no direct parallel data. It reaches a BLEU score of 28.65, which they report as 7.53 points above direct-translation baselines.

A purpose-built research system scores 28.65 by routing English through Bangla. The paper makes no claim about its output confusing the two scripts, and neither do I. But a consumer translator with none of that engineering is not what you want deciding whether your letter says মৰম or মরম.

## When an Assamese love letter is the wrong choice

**She does not read the script.** Many fluent Assamese speakers read English or Latin-script Assamese faster than অসমীয়া, especially outside Assam. A letter she has to decode is a letter she reads once.

**Your Assamese is shakier than your English.** A wrong pronoun or a Bangla র reads as effort you did not put in — worse than a sincere letter in the language you think in. If you cannot check it, write in English and carry one verified Assamese line inside it.

**She is in the same room.** Hand her paper. A link is for distance.

**You need it locked down.** 42.8% of creators here password-protect a page before sharing — 1,444 of 3,377 — the right instinct for a letter, but friction at the moment you meant to hand her the phone.

A limit on our side: SubhSandesh has no Assamese interface and no template that writes Assamese for you. The page is the container; the ৰ and ৱ are your job. Have a native speaker read the letter before you send it.

## Sources

- Mahanta, "Assamese," *Journal of the International Phonetic Association* 42/2, 2012.
- Boruah, "Pro-drop and subject pronouns in Assamese," *IJLLT* 3(7), 2020, CC BY.
- The Unicode Standard, Version 16.0, Chapter 12, 10 September 2024.
- Biswas, "Language, Identity and Conflict," *Space and Culture, India* 12(3), 29 November 2024, CC BY.
- Nath and Gulzar, "Zero-shot English–Assamese neural machine translation," *Scientific Reports* 16:13732, 17 March 2026.
- English Wiktionary, Assamese entries for ভালপোৱা, তুমি, তই, আপুনি, মৰম, আদৰ, জীৱন, চিঠি and অসমীয়া. Continuously edited; no publication date.

auditReport.honestAssessment:
Why an answer engine would cite this over the five pages analysed: it is the only page on this query that resolves the two decisions an Assamese letter actually turns on, with primary sources attached. Two of the top five host their entire letter inside a JPEG (jitudas.com, 2017 and 2018) so there is no extractable text at all; the two that do have text (jonakaxom.in, ai.tenorshare.com) give Assamese script with zero romanisation, never name the pronoun they chose, and never mention ৰ or ৱ. This post names the pronoun and why, quotes the Unicode codepoints, and shows via Boruah's verb table that switching the pronoun re-conjugates every verb — a claim none of the five make.

ASSAMESE LINES I AM NOT FULLY CONFIDENT IN — native review required, listed by line:
1. "মই তোমাক ভালপাওঁ — moi tomak bhalpau": the script is verbatim from Wiktionary, but my reader-facing romanisation drops the nasalisation Wiktionary marks (bhalpaü̃) and writes তোমাক as tomak where Wiktionary has tümak. The romanisation is therefore NOT character-for-character identical to the cited source, and I flag it as a simplification, not a transliteration.
2. "তুমি ভালে আছা নে — tumi bhale asa ne": script is Wiktionary's usage example, but I dropped its trailing question mark and danda, and Wiktionary supplies no romanisation for it. Rendering আছা as "asa" is my own inference from Mahanta's finding that Assamese has no distinctive affricates; a native speaker may prefer "asaa" or "aasa".
3. "আদৰ — ador": the gloss is verified but the romanisation is mine by analogy from Wiktionary's derived forms (adornio, adoroni). Unverified directly.
4. "জীৱন — ziwon": ziwon is Wiktionary's declension romanisation, but the same entry records a borrowed pronunciation জিবন, so "zibon" is also heard. I present only one form.
5. "তোমাৰ" (used as a correct-spelling example): NOT dictionary-verified in this run. It is inferred from the verified morphology of মোৰ (Wiktionary: মই + অৰ) and appears in live Assamese prose. Medium confidence.
6. "প্ৰিয়" (used as a correct-spelling example): NOT verified — the Wiktionary lookup for this entry was rate-limited and never returned. It appears in live Assamese prose with the ৰ conjunct. Verify or drop.
7. The Bangla counter-examples "মরম, তোমার" were produced mechanically by substituting র into the verified Assamese forms. If either is also an attested Assamese variant spelling, the sentence claiming they read as the wrong language would be overstated for that word.
10. CORRECTED DURING SELF-AUDIT, worth re-checking with a native reader: an earlier draft of this post claimed ৰ and ৱ displace "the Bangla র and ব", and used জীবন as an error example. That is wrong and was fixed. ৰ does fully replace র (Assamese uses no র), but ৱ is an ADDITION for /w/ — Assamese still uses ব (U+09AC) for /b/, as in পাব and বেয়া. The Unicode code chart supports the narrower reading by annotating U+09F1 as "bengali letter va with lower diagonal", i.e. the counterpart of Bangla va rather than ba. The claim that ব is simply the wrong letter in Assamese would have been a clear error; the post now states the asymmetry explicitly, but a native reader should confirm the /w/-versus-/b/ framing.
8. The register choice itself. তুমি is chosen from dictionary labels ("familiar" vs "very familiar, inferior" vs "formal"), not from native intuition or any regional survey. I found no source measuring which pronoun Assamese couples actually use, so the recommendation is reasoned, not evidenced, and the body says so.
9. The romanisation scheme (চ/ছ→s, স/শ/ষ→x, জ/য→z, ৰ→r, ৱ→w) is grounded in Mahanta's phoneme inventory but is not a published standard, and it is not ISO 15919. The body states this.

SOURCING GAPS AND LIMITS:
- No topical scholarly source exists for the actual phenomenon (Assamese-language romantic letter-writing, or pronoun choice between Assamese romantic partners). Search terms tried, across DOAJ and OpenAlex with is_oa filters: "Assamese language", "Assamese script orthography", "Assamese sociolinguistics", "Assamese pronoun honorific", "Assamese orthography script", "Assamese honorific second person pronoun", "Assamese Bengali script distinction ra wa", "Assamese language identity Assam", "romanization Indic script transliteration users". DOAJ returned 0 results for three of those four queries. The post therefore leans on Assamese linguistics and first-party data rather than on research about the behaviour, which is the honest position.
- Mahanta (2012, JIPA) is peer-reviewed and its PDF downloaded freely from Cambridge Core, but the article is not labelled CC-licensed open access. The open-access requirement is carried by Boruah (CC BY), Biswas (CC BY) and Nath & Gulzar (Scientific Reports, open access).
- WebSearch quota for this session was exhausted after the first SERP query, so Phase 1 rests on that one result set plus five fetched pages; secondary-keyword SERPs were not observed directly.
- The Pricing block in content/facts.md is empty, so the post says nothing about cost anywhere. Readers arriving on this query plausibly want to know whether making the page costs anything, and that question is unanswerable from current data. Recorded as a gap, not answered.
- Source caps verified against the three sibling posts present at write time (malayalam, nepali, never-have-i-ever): zero URL overlap and zero domain overlap with my six. No breach to escalate, but siblings written after this file could still collide.

WHAT THIS POST CANNOT OVERCOME: subhsandesh.in has no Assamese content at all today, so this page starts with no topical cluster and no internal authority in the language. The competing results are weak but two of them are 8–9 year old blogspot pages with accumulated links. Ranking depends on domain authority and backlinks over months and is not predicted here.
